description: The closing ballad of Boylan Heights — the Raleigh band's Mitch Easter-produced second album, named for the historic Raleigh neighborhood it quietly elegizes.

pops.text: This is the closing track — track 11 — on Boylan Heights, the Connells' second album, released in 1987.
All the songs on Boylan Heights were written by guitarist Mike Connell, except 'Home Today' by George Huntley.
Producer Mitch Easter was the R.E.M. connection — he'd produced Murmur and Reckoning, and comparisons followed the Connells for years.
It was recorded at Easter's Drive-In Studio in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.
The album is named for Boylan Heights, a historic neighborhood in the band's hometown of Raleigh, North Carolina.
Band lore calls this closing ballad a haunting tribute to that same Raleigh neighborhood.
Mike Connell formed the band in 1984 with his brother David on bass, Doug MacMillan on vocals, and future filmmaker John Schultz on drums.
Boylan Heights was the band's first album for TVT Records — after the major labels, including Columbia, passed on it.
TVT had made its name with 'Tee Vee Toons' TV-theme compilations — an unlikely home for a jangle-pop classic.
The album became a substantial college-radio hit, and its songs formed the foundation of the Connells' live show for the rest of their career.

title: I Suppose

description: A brooding, slow-burning track from Now and Zen — Plant's 1988 comeback album, where his new band meets a couple of famous guest solos from Jimmy Page elsewhere on the record.

pops.text: From Now and Zen, released in February 1988 on Plant's own Es Paranza label through Atlantic.
It was co-written by Plant, keyboardist Phil Johnstone, and guitarist Doug Boyle — the core of Plant's new late-'80s band.
The album was recorded in late 1987 at Swanyard Studios and Marcus Studios in London.
Producers were Plant, Johnstone, and Tim Palmer, who gave the record its polished, atmospheric sheen.
Released as a single in November 1988, it peaked at #46 on Billboard's US rock chart.
Jimmy Page guests on two other album tracks — 'Heaven Knows' and 'Tall Cool One' — but the guitar here is Doug Boyle's.
Now and Zen generated two Mainstream Rock #1s: 'Heaven Knows' for six weeks and 'Tall Cool One' for four.
Backing vocalists on the album include Kirsty MacColl, Marie Pierre, and Toni Halliday, later of Curve.
The album earned Plant his first solo multi-platinum certification in the US — his biggest solo success to that point.
At 5 minutes 39 seconds, it's one of the longest, most spacious tracks on the album — a slow burn amid the hits.

title: The Way I Feel

description: Madonna's euphoric title track from Ray of Light — Jonas Åkerlund's time-lapse video of a day on Earth, and the record that reinvented her as an electronica artist.

pops.text: The title track of Madonna's seventh studio album, released as its second single in May 1998.
It was built with producer William Orbit from a 1970s folk song, 'Sepheryn,' by Curtiss Maldoon — Dave Curtiss and Christine Leach.
Leach, Orbit's niece, sings the original melody the track grew from; she shares a co-writing credit.
Director Jonas Åkerlund's video compresses a whole day — subways, bowling, city crowds — into frantic time-lapse.
The video won Video of the Year at the 1998 MTV Video Music Awards, plus Best Female Video.
The song itself won the Grammy for Best Dance Recording, and the video won Best Short Form Music Video.
It peaked at #5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and #2 in the UK, and topped the US dance chart.
Madonna had recently become a mother and studied Kabbalah and yoga — the album's spiritual glow starts here.
Orbit's bubbling synths and breakbeats marked Madonna's full turn into electronica — a career reinvention at 39.
The Ray of Light album won four Grammys and is regularly ranked among the greatest albums of the 1990s.

title: Ray of Light

description: The first single from the Denver funk project's self-titled 2014 debut — Jordan Linit and Josh Fairman plus the Shady Horns, recorded on vintage gear at Scanhope Sound in Colorado.

pops.text: This was Analog Son's first released single, ahead of their self-titled debut album in 2014.
The band is the brainchild of guitarist Jordan Linit and bassist Josh Fairman, friends and bandmates for years in Kinetix.
They recorded the album over months at Scanhope Sound in Morrison, Colorado — near Red Rocks — using vintage equipment.
Fairman co-founded Scanhope Sound in 2012 with Joel Scanlon, on the steps of Red Rocks Amphitheatre.
Those horns are the Shady Horns — Ryan Zoidis and Eric Bloom of Lettuce and Soulive fame.
New Mastersounds keyboardist Joe Tatton is in the mix too — reviewers singled out his soloing trade-offs with Linit here.
The wider cast includes Ivan Neville of Dumpstaphunk and Joey Porter of The Motet.
At 7 minutes 33 seconds, it's the debut album's long, loose showcase track — part composed funk, part jam vehicle.
Drummer Mike Marlier drives it on hi-hat while the horns ride the melody, per Jazz Weekly's review.
The band's name is the concept: the 'son' of analog — vintage tape-era funk made by a digital-age studio project.

title: Analog Island

description: John Fogerty's two-minute blast against draft-era privilege — released in 1969, and given its first-ever official music video in 2018 for CCR's 50th anniversary, directed by Ben Fee.

pops.text: Released in November 1969 on Willy and the Poor Boys, CCR's fourth album in under two years.
John Fogerty wrote it in a fury — he said the song poured out in about 20 minutes.
Fogerty had been drafted himself in 1966 and served in the Army Reserve — he knew exactly who did and didn't go.
The target: the 'fortunate sons' of senators and millionaires who could dodge the Vietnam draft.
It was the B-side of 'Down on the Corner' — and the double-sided single peaked at #3 on the Hot 100.
On its own chart run as part of that single, 'Fortunate Son' reached #14 in the US.
Rolling Stone placed it among the 500 greatest songs of all time, and it entered the National Recording Registry in 2013.
This video arrived in 2018 — the song's first official video, nearly 49 years after release, directed by Ben Fee.
Fee road-tripped across America filming working-class families dancing, working, and driving — 'It ain't me' made visual.
The video launched Craft Recordings' CCR50 campaign celebrating 50 years since the band's 1968 debut.

title: Fortunate Son

description: The opener of V. — the San Francisco psych quartet's fifth album, written by Ripley Johnson in the smoky summer of 2017 as a laid-back antidote to wildfires and dread.

pops.text: 'Eclipse' opens V., Wooden Shjips' fifth album, released May 25, 2018 on Thrill Jockey Records.
It was the band's first album in five years, following 2013's Back to Land.
Guitarist-singer Ripley Johnson wrote the album in summer 2017 as an antidote to political anxiety and Pacific Northwest wildfires.
Johnson spent that summer on his Portland porch as ash fell like snow — that apocalyptic haze hangs over the record.
The quartet: Johnson, Dusty Jermier on bass, Omar Ahsanuddin on drums, and Nash Whalen on keyboards.
That smoky saxophone is guest Rob Frye, weaving around Johnson's reverb-thick guitar.
Between Shjips albums, Johnson kept busy with Moon Duo, his project with keyboardist Sanae Yamada.
Critics heard V. as the band taking Spacemen 3's place as premium hypnotic, psychedelic riff machines.
The whole album is just seven tracks across 42 minutes — every song gets room to unwind.
Yes, the 'j' is intentional: it's pronounced 'Ships' — the spelling is a nod to a misspelled concert poster.

title: Eclipse

description: The Cure's sunniest single, from Wish — Tim Pope's chaotic Méliès-inspired video has the gloomiest band in Britain grinning, dancing, and trashing the set.

pops.text: The second single from Wish (1992) — and the most unabashedly happy song Robert Smith ever wrote.
Smith wrote it as a deliberate antidote — a pure pop song for people who'd forgotten how good Fridays feel.
It was recorded in D major but sped up slightly with vari-speed in production, landing it between pitches.
Smith was so pleased with the melody he worried he'd subconsciously stolen it, and rang people humming it to check.
Tim Pope's video pays homage to French silent-film pioneer Georges Méliès and his 1907 film The Eclipse.
Pope opens the video himself — riding a rocking horse, shouting directions through a megaphone after inhaling helium.
The final shot: bassist Simon Gallup crouching at the camera in a bridal veil, holding champagne.
The video won European Viewer's Choice for Best Music Video at the 1992 MTV Video Music Awards.
It hit #6 in the UK and #18 on the Hot 100, and topped Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart.
Wish became the Cure's highest-charting album in the US, reaching #2 on the Billboard 200.

title: Friday I'm in Love

description: The lead single from The Alien Coast — the Birmingham soul band trading vintage R&B for synth-driven apocalyptic dance-pop, with dancer Liv Mai leading the video.

pops.text: Released October 5, 2021 as the lead single from The Alien Coast, the band's fourth album and ATO Records debut.
Frontman Paul Janeway: the song is about 'dancing while facing certain doom — like dancing through a Mad Max scene.'
Bassist Jesse Phillips originally composed the beat and bassline that anchor the track.
The video was directed by Machete Bang Bang, whose credits include work with Coldplay and Evan Rachel Wood.
Lead dancer Liv Mai's credits include Euphoria, Transparent, and Crazy Ex-Girlfriend.
The Alien Coast was recorded in the band's hometown of Birmingham, Alabama, and released January 28, 2022.
The band described the album as a 'fever dream convergence of soul and psychedelia' — synths and samples over their soul roots.
The eight-piece formed in Birmingham in 2011 when Janeway, a former bank teller, teamed up with Phillips.
They performed this song live on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert the night before the album's release.
A separate live video was filmed in a single take at Ol Elegante Studios in Birmingham, where the band made early recordings.

title: The Last Dance

description: Cooke's two-minute charmer about knowing nothing about history — or biology, or a science book — but knowing he loves you, seen here in its official lyric video.

pops.text: Released April 14, 1960 on Keen Records — Cooke's biggest hit since 'You Send Me' in 1957.
It was written by Lou Adler and Herb Alpert, then revised by Cooke, who reshaped the lyric around school subjects.
The three writers were credited under the pseudonym 'Barbara Campbell' — the name of Cooke's high-school sweetheart.
Herb Alpert went on to Tijuana Brass fame and co-founded A&M Records two years later, in 1962.
It peaked at #12 on the Billboard Hot 100 and #2 on the R&B chart in 1960.
The whole performance runs barely over two minutes — a masterclass in saying it all, fast.
In 1986 it re-entered the UK chart and hit #2, after soundtracking a famous Levi's 501 jeans commercial.
Herman's Hermits took their own version to #4 in the US in 1965.
Art Garfunkel, Paul Simon, and James Taylor recorded it together in 1978 — three voices, one standard.
Rolling Stone ranked it among the 500 greatest songs of all time. There is no known film of Cooke performing it — hence this lyric video.

title: (What A) Wonderful World

description: The opening track of Hot Damn!, the Leeds funk band's 2007 debut on First Word Records — a horn-driven entrance theme, presented here in the label's official stream.

pops.text: Track 1 of Hot Damn!, the Haggis Horns' debut album, released October 1, 2007 on First Word Records (catalogue FW016).
The band is from Leeds, England — at the forefront of the UK funk scene with a self-described 'northern funk' sound.
Their sound combines heavy breakbeat funk, soul, hip-hop, and afrobeat, played by trained jazz musicians.
The core horn section — Malcolm Strachan, Atholl Ransome, and Ben Barker — became one of Britain's most in-demand brass teams.
First Word released the track with a couple of the band's live-show cover staples alongside their originals on Hot Damn!.
This is the label's official stream, distributed by Kudos Records — the band's own entrance music, horns first.
Band members have performed and recorded with artists including The Cinematic Orchestra and Lou Donaldson.
The Haggis Horns later launched their own imprint, Haggis Records, for albums like One of These Days (2017).
Two decades on, the band is still a live powerhouse — an eight-piece funk extravaganza on stage.
The title is a play on Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon — a kung-fu entrance for Scotland's national dish.

title: Enter the Haggis

description: Track two of Chronic Town, R.E.M.'s 1982 debut EP — Michael Stipe's 'first real song,' a jangling mystery inspired by a neighbor who gardened at 2 a.m. in a suit and tie.

pops.text: From Chronic Town, R.E.M.'s debut EP, released August 24, 1982 on I.R.S. Records.
Michael Stipe told Rolling Stone in 1992: 'We didn't really write a song until Gardening at Night.' He calls it their first real song.
Peter Buck has said it was inspired by an old man in his Athens neighborhood who gardened at 2 a.m. wearing a suit and tie.
It was produced by Mitch Easter and the band at Easter's Drive-In Studio in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.
The band named their publishing company Night Garden Music after this song.
It's the second of just five songs on Chronic Town, following the opener 'Wolves, Lower.'
A different vocal mix appeared on the 1988 I.R.S. compilation Eponymous — Stipe's singing is noticeably clearer.
A slow, country-style version recorded around Reckoning surfaced officially on the 2006 compilation And I Feel Fine.
Chronic Town never got a standalone CD release until its 40th anniversary reissue in August 2022.
The EP preceded their debut album Murmur by a year — the whole R.E.M. sound is already here in miniature.

title: Gardening At Night

description: The closing track of Some Girls — Keith's riff and 'sha-doobie' hook under Mick's rapid-fire portrait of a rat-infested, dope-ridden, gloriously alive 1978 New York City.

pops.text: The closing track of Some Girls (1978), the Stones' best-selling album in the United States.
Keith Richards came up with the guitar riff, the title, and the 'sha-doobie' refrain; Mick Jagger wrote the rest.
It was recorded at Pathé Marconi Studios in Paris across sessions from October 1977 to March 1978.
Jagger barely sings it — he half-raps the verses, a nod to the punk and New York street energy of the moment.
Some Girls was the first album with Ronnie Wood as a full-time member — his guitar weaves with Keith's throughout.
Released as a US single in late 1978, it peaked at #31 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Its B-side, 'Everything Is Turning to Gold,' was a non-album track co-written with Ronnie Wood.
The Stones performed it on Saturday Night Live in October 1978 — a famously loose set where Jagger licked Wood's face mid-song.
The lyric is a love-hate postcard to New York: money, rats, garbage, and a city that still speeds on by.
Some Girls was widely seen as the Stones' answer to punk and disco — and 'Shattered' is its punkest moment.

title: Shattered

description: A swampy blues-funk tale from Gravel Road Grooves — promptgenix's 2026 album, presented in the artist's full-song lyric video about something lurking in the Massachusetts woods.

pops.text: Track 4 on Gravel Road Grooves, promptgenix's eight-track album released March 16, 2026.
The album came out on the independent label 10302836 Records DK and is classified as blues.
The track runs 4 minutes 36 seconds — one of the album's longer cuts.
Songwriting and production are credited to C T C, the name behind the promptgenix project.
The artist's own video bills this as the 'Full song & Lyrics' version, tagged blues, funk, and folk music.
The title points to Grafton, a town in Worcester County, Massachusetts — classic New England woods for a creature tale.
A week after release, San Francisco's KXSF-LP spun it on The Everything Show with Dan Carlisle, March 23, 2026.
A 2026 Medium 'Digital Testament' essay read the song's headless monster as a warning about capitalism run wild.
The album's other titles set the scene: 'The River Got Teeth,' 'Red Eyes Over Point Pleasant,' and 'Engines of the Deep.'
By October 2026, another promptgenix track, 'Nobody's Keeping Score,' sat at #1 on South Africa's Apple Music blues chart.

title: The Thing in Grafton Woods

description: One of Panic's oldest originals — debuted in Athens in 1986 and released on their 1991 self-titled album — seen here in the band's official pro-shot Red Rocks performance from June 25, 2023.

pops.text: This official pro-shot footage comes from Widespread Panic's Sunday show at Red Rocks on June 25, 2023.
'C. Brown' is a co-write between the band and Jeff Riley.
It's one of Panic's oldest originals — debuted February 13, 1986 at the Uptown Lounge in Athens, Georgia, per Everyday Companion.
The song later appeared on the band's 1991 self-titled album for Capricorn Records, as track 7.
By this Red Rocks performance, the band had played the song 805 times.
At Red Rocks 2023 it fell second in the first set, right after the opener 'Up All Night.'
John Bell sings lead, as he has since the Athens bar-band days when the song was new.
The 2023 lineup features guitarist Jimmy Herring and drummer Duane Trucks alongside Bell, Dave Schools, Domingo Ortiz, and JoJo Hermann.
Founding guitarist Michael Houser, who played on the 1991 recording, died in 2002 — the song remains a living link to him.
Red Rocks is Panic's home away from home — they've sold out the venue dozens of times across four decades.

title: C. Brown

description: Weir and Hunter's tale of two drifters out of Wichita — performed at the Veneta, Oregon creamery benefit on August 27, 1972, in the official Sunshine Daydream live video.

pops.text: You're watching the Veneta, Oregon performance of August 27, 1972, from the film Sunshine Daydream.
The show was a benefit for the Springfield Creamery, owned by Chuck Kesey — brother of novelist Ken Kesey.
'Jack Straw' was written by Bob Weir and Robert Hunter, who trade the story of two drifters, Shannon and Jack Straw.
Weir and Jerry Garcia split the vocals, each singing one drifter's lines — a duet in character.
The song was first performed live on October 19, 1971 in Minneapolis — Keith Godchaux's first show with the band.
Its first release came on the triple live album Europe '72, recorded that spring at the Olympia Theatre in Paris and elsewhere.
Europe '72 was released in November 1972 and became the Dead's first gold album.
The Veneta show drew some 20,000 people to the Old Renaissance Faire Grounds in brutal summer heat.
Sunshine Daydream footage sat largely unseen for decades before its official release at Meet Up at the Movies in August 2013.
The song became a signature first-set opener for the rest of the Dead's career — usually a sign the jam would stretch out.

title: Jack Straw
